l: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, The MIRAGE Benchmark / Evaluation Settings .. Component Datasets
s: The MIRAGE Benchmark evaluates retrieval-augmented generation systems for medical question answering under four settings: zero-shot learning, multi-choice evaluation, retrieval-augmented generation, and question-only retrieval. It contains 7,663 biomedical multi-choice questions from five datasets: MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, MedMCQA, PubMedQA*, and BioASQ-Y/N. The benchmark excludes ground-truth supporting contexts and evaluates systems by answer-choice accuracy, standard deviation, and the average accuracy across all five tasks.

l: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, The MEDRAG Toolkit
s: The MEDRAG Toolkit is introduced as a toolkit for systematically evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems for medical question answering on the MIRAGE benchmark. It contains three components: Corpora, Retrievers, and LLMs, and includes PubMed, StatPearls, Textbooks, Wikipedia, and the combined MedCorp corpus. Its retrievers include BM25, Contriever, SPECTER, and MedCPT, while its language models include GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Mixtral, Llama-2, MEDITRON, and PMC-LLaMA. On the MIRAGE benchmark, MEDRAG generally improves average accuracy over chain-of-thought without retrieval, with GPT-4 achieving the highest MEDRAG average of 79.97%.

s: GPT-4 is a closed, general-domain language model with a 32,768-token context length in MEDRAG. Its chain-of-thought baseline has a 73.44% average accuracy on MIRAGE, while MEDRAG reaches 79.97%, the highest average among the listed models.

l: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: The unit evaluates MEDRAG on the MIRAGE benchmark across backbone LLMs, corpora, retrievers, snippet counts, and context positions. GPT-4 performs best with chain-of-thought prompting, while MEDRAG substantially improves GPT-3.5 and Mixtral and can make them comparable to GPT-4 under chain-of-thought prompting. PubMed and MedCorp are the most broadly useful corpora, with MedCPT, BM25, and reciprocal rank fusion providing strong retrieval options. The results show that medical question answering depends on task-specific corpus selection, retrieval quality, snippet quantity, and snippet placement.

l: MEDRAG, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MEDRAG is evaluated on MIRAGE with different LLMs, corpora, retrievers, numbers of retrieved snippets, and context positions. It substantially improves several backbone models, performs best broadly with PubMed or MedCorp, and can suffer when too few or too many snippets are supplied.

l: MIRAGE, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MIRAGE is used to compare medical question-answering systems across MMLU-Med, MedQA-US, MedMCQA, PubMedQA*, and BioASQ-Y/N. Its results support recommendations for corpus, retriever, LLM, snippet-count, and context-arrangement choices.

l: retrieval-augmented generation, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Retrieval-augmented generation is shown to improve the zero-shot medical question-answering capability of LLMs and may be more efficient than larger-scale pre-training. Its effectiveness depends on finding useful medical information and maintaining an adequate signal-to-noise ratio in the retrieved context.

l: chain-of-thought prompting, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Chain-of-thought prompting is used as the non-retrieval comparison setting. GPT-4 achieves 73.44% average accuracy under this setting, while domain-specific models can outperform it on selected tasks such as PubMedQA*.

l: GPT-4, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: GPT-4 significantly outperforms the other compared models with chain-of-thought prompting, averaging 73.44% on MIRAGE and approximately 80% according to the practical recommendations. It is described as the strongest model but more expensive than alternatives.

l: GPT-3.5, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: GPT-3.5 benefits substantially from MEDRAG, reaching around 70% average performance and showing the greatest reported improvement from MEDRAG (+17.9%). It is recommended as a more cost-efficient alternative to GPT-4 because it follows MEDRAG instructions effectively.

l: Mixtral, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Mixtral averages 61.42% across the five MIRAGE tasks with chain-of-thought prompting, slightly exceeding GPT-3.5 in that setting. MEDRAG improves its performance to around 70%, although GPT-3.5 with MEDRAG remains 3.0% better; Mixtral is also presented as a viable locally deployable option for privacy-sensitive scenarios.

l: MedCorp, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MedCorp is a 65.3-million-item combination of the evaluated corpora and provides robust performance across MIRAGE tasks. With GPT-3.5 and RRF-4, it reaches a 71.57% average accuracy, and both RRF-2 and RRF-4 are recommended as reliable retrieval choices.

l: PubMed, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: PubMed is a 23.9-million-item corpus and the only single corpus besides MedCorp that improves performance on all MIRAGE tasks. It is especially useful for PubMedQA* and BioASQ-Y/N, and RRF-2 combining BM25 and MedCPT is recommended for this corpus.

l: BM25, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: BM25 is a strong individual retriever across the experiments. It is recommended as part of the RRF-2 combination with MedCPT for PubMed.

l: MedCPT, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MedCPT is a biomedical retriever trained on PubMed user logs. It performs particularly well with PubMed and is described as the most reliable of the four individual retrievers, while also being recommended alongside BM25 in RRF-2.

l: Reciprocal Rank Fusion, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Reciprocal rank fusion combines retrieval results from multiple retrievers and generally improves robustness and performance. RRF-4 achieves 71.57% average accuracy with MedCorp, but adding a poorly performing retriever can hurt performance, so the choice of fused retrievers must be made cautiously.

l: MMLU-Med, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MMLU-Med is one of the five MIRAGE tasks. Textbooks with RRF-2 achieve its highest reported accuracy of 76.68%, while medical examination tasks generally retrieve more snippets from Textbooks and StatPearls.

l: MedQA-US, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MedQA-US is one of the MIRAGE examination tasks. StatPearls with Contriever reaches the highest reported accuracy of 67.48%, and Textbooks constitute a relatively large share of retrieved snippets for this task.

l: MedMCQA, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: MedMCQA is one of the five MIRAGE tasks and receives limited benefit from any single corpus. MedCorp nevertheless improves the performance of almost all retrievers on this task, by between -1.5% and +5.0% as reported.

l: PubMedQA*, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: PubMedQA* is a research-related MIRAGE task that benefits strongly from PubMed because supporting literature can be retrieved there. MEDRAG can achieve high accuracy with one snippet, but performance decreases as more irrelevant snippets are added; 79.6% of ground-truth snippets are identified as the top-ranked context.

l: BioASQ-Y/N, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: BioASQ-Y/N is a research-related MIRAGE task that benefits primarily from PubMed. Unlike PubMedQA*, its accuracy rises substantially as more snippets are supplied, and it can also benefit from reciprocal rank fusion when individual retrievers perform poorly.

l: medical question answering, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Medical question answering is improved by retrieval-augmented generation, particularly when the corpus matches the question type. Examination questions tend to benefit from Textbooks and StatPearls, whereas research-related questions benefit from PubMed.

l: retrieved snippets, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Results .. Practical Recommendations
s: Retrieved snippets provide useful medical information but can hinder performance when too few are available or when excessive irrelevant content lowers the signal-to-noise ratio. Their ordering also matters: accuracy shows a U-shaped pattern as the ground-truth snippet moves through the context, consistent with a lost-in-the-middle effect.

l: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine, Limitations
s: The study on MEDRAG systematically evaluates medical RAG systems and provides practical recommendations. It mainly evaluates the vanilla RAG architecture, in which retrieved documents are directly prepended to the LLM context, while leaving newer designs such as active RAG for future work. The study identifies limitations involving corpus coverage, retrieval evaluation, examination datasets, and the use of multiple-choice QA. It also notes that MEDRAG could support other knowledge-intensive tasks and that its generated rationales remain to be evaluated.

l: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, Abstract
s: The unit introduces ARES, an Automated RAG Evaluation System for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems. ARES creates synthetic training data and finetunes lightweight language-model judges to assess context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance. It uses a small set of human-annotated datapoints for prediction-powered inference to mitigate prediction errors. Across eight knowledge-intensive tasks in KILT, SuperGLUE, and AIS, ARES accurately evaluates systems using only a few hundred human annotations and remains effective across domain shifts.

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, Introduction
s: A RAG system typically consists of a retriever and a downstream language model (LM). Given a user question, its retriever finds relevant passages from a corpus and its language model uses those passages to generate a response. Its design involves choices such as the retrieval model, how documents are divided into retrieval chunks, and how the language model is prompted or fine-tuned to use the retrieved information.

l: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, opening
s: The unit introduces ARES, an automated system for evaluating RAG systems across context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance. ARES uses an LM to generate synthetic question–answer data, fine-tunes lightweight judges for three classification tasks, and applies prediction-powered inference with a small human preference validation set to produce scores and confidence intervals. It requires an in-domain passage set, approximately 150 or more annotated validation examples, and a few in-domain query–answer examples. Across reported experiments, ARES outperforms RAGAS and other approaches in evaluation accuracy and reduces annotation requirements by 78% compared with an annotation-based baseline.

l: ARES, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, opening

l: Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, opening

l: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES .. 3.3
s: ARES evaluates and ranks RAG systems in three stages: synthetic data generation, LLM judge training, and prediction-powered inference. s: Context relevance measures whether a passage returned for a query is relevant for answering that query. Its negative examples use unrelated passages as weak negatives and passages from the same document, or BM25-retrieved similar passages, as strong negatives.

s: Answer faithfulness measures whether an answer is faithful to the retrieved passage rather than containing hallucinated or extrapolated statements. Its negative examples include answers generated from other passages and answers prompted to be contradictory.

s: The Kendall rank correlation coefficient, or Kendall's tau, measures the correlation between the correct ranking and the ARES ranking by comparing concordant and discordant pairs. A value greater than 0.9 is considered successful, with the coefficient ranging from 0.0 to 1.0.

s: The experiments construct mock RAG systems with known positive and negative query-passage and query-passage-answer examples. Nine dataset splits represent systems with success rates from 70% to 90%, separated by 2.5 percentage points, allowing ARES to be tested on scoring and ranking.

l: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems, Results & Analysis / 5.1 .. 5.4
s: This unit evaluates ARES against RAGAS and GPT-3.5 for ranking RAG systems and scoring context relevance, answer relevance, and answer faithfulness. ARES generally achieves higher Kendall’s tau and accuracy than the baselines, uses PPI to improve predictions and provide confidence intervals, and requires fewer human annotations than sampled annotation methods. s: ARES ranks RAG systems more accurately than RAGAS and the GPT-3.5 judge across the evaluated KILT and SuperGLUE datasets, with PPI improving its fine-tuned LLM judge. s: KILT supplies datasets used to evaluate ARES across pseudo RAG systems and existing RAG systems, including NQ, Wizards of Wikipedia, FEVER, and T-Rex. ARES shows strong performance across the evaluated KILT settings but has limited generalization for the extraction task represented by T-Rex.

s: Kendall’s tau measures how accurately methods rank RAG systems. s: ARES provides more accurate RAG system ranking than RAGAS, GPT-3.5, and sampled annotations in the reported experiments. It is also used to guide decisions about document splitting, retriever selection, and generative LLM choice.

s: Human annotations are used for PPI validation and for comparison with sampled annotation methods. ARES achieves more accurate ranking than sampled annotations while using 78% fewer annotations, and experiments indicate that 150 annotations are the minimum number required in one setting.

s: The unit examines retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) approaches and combinations for enhancing large language models. It finds that existing query-dependent retrieval methods can be complex to implement and can prolong response times. Through extensive experiments, the authors propose RAG deployment strategies that balance performance and efficiency. The unit also reports that multimodal retrieval techniques improve question-answering about visual inputs and accelerate multimodal content generation through a "retrieval as generation" strategy.

l: Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Introduction
s: The introduction explains that generative large language models can produce outdated information or fabricated facts, while retrieval-augmented generation combines pretrained models with retrieval to improve robustness and enable domain-specific applications without updating model parameters. It describes the RAG workflow, including query classification, retrieval, reranking, repacking, summarization, document chunking, embedding selection, vector databases, and LLM fine-tuning. The study systematically compares RAG methods and combinations to identify practices that balance effectiveness and efficiency across application scenarios. It also presents an evaluation framework and reports that multimodal retrieval can improve visual question answering and accelerate multimodal content generation through retrieval as generation.

s: The unit concerns the accuracy of responses generated by Large Language Models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and LLaMA. It states that increasing model size does not fundamentally solve hallucinations, particularly in knowledge-intensive and specialized-domain tasks. Retrieval-augmented generation addresses these challenges by retrieving relevant documents from external knowledge bases to provide accurate, real-time, domain-specific context. Prior work has improved the RAG pipeline through query and retrieval transformations, retriever and generator fine-tuning, and better interaction among queries, retrieval, and generation.

l: Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Query and Retrieval Transformation
s: The section on Query and Retrieval Transformation explains that effective retrieval depends on accurate, clear, and detailed queries, although semantic differences between queries and relevant documents can remain after embedding conversion. It describes query transformation methods, including Query2Doc and HyDE, which generate pseudo-documents, and TOC, which decomposes queries into subqueries and aggregates retrieved content. It also discusses transforming retrieval source documents through LlamaIndex-generated pseudo-queries and contrastive learning, as well as post-processing retrieved documents with summarization and compression techniques. These approaches aim to improve query-document matching, retrieval performance, generator output, and context efficiency.

Surveys cover RAG applications in text generation, LLM integration, multimodal systems, and AI-generated content, but selecting an appropriate algorithm for practical implementation remains difficult.
